My name is Bruno, and for thirty years I have driven the same road along this coast, the narrow one, with the sea on your left and the rock on your right. Every passenger who sits behind me asks me the same question, sooner or later: what should we see? And for the first ten years I gave them a list. Ten places, twelve places, everything in the book. Then I understood something. A list is not an answer. A good answer is one opinion and one reason, and nothing more. I would rather tell you one thing that is worth your morning than ten things you will forget before lunch. So here is mine. The famous beach, the one on every postcard, the one everybody photographs: it is a little overrated. In August it is too crowded, the sand is not big enough for the people who are standing on it, and you will spend two hours in a line to sit in somebody else's shadow. Honestly? I would skip it. Take the early boat instead, at eight, before the water gets busy, and look at this coast from the sea. That is the way it was built to be seen. And one more thing, from thirty years of driving. Some people arrive with the guidebook open and they leave with the guidebook closed, and every single thing they did was in it. Their trip was fine. But it was somebody else's trip. The passengers who come back to me years later, who remember my name, are always the ones who took one honest recommendation from a real person. Nobody has ever told me they remember a guidebook. They remember a stranger at breakfast who said: if I were you, I would go here.

I am Diane, I am seventy years old, and for most of my life every place I visited was nice. That was my word. The cathedral was nice. The dinner was nice. Venice, Prague, Seville: all of them nice. I saw so much more than I could ever say, and because I had only that one word, I sounded like a woman with no opinions at all. People stopped asking me about my trips, and I understood why. Nobody wants to hear that everything was nice. And then, two years ago, in a small hotel in Seville, a young couple sat down at the table next to mine with a map, and the girl turned to me and asked where they should eat that night. I almost said it. I almost said everything here is nice. But I stopped, and I tried. I said the restaurants on the square were pricey, and a bit touristy, and that if I were them, I would walk two streets behind the church and eat where the local families eat, and go late, because nobody in Spain eats at seven. Six or seven sentences. My hands were cold the whole time. The next morning they came to my table before I had finished my coffee, and they told me it was the best dinner of their trip. And I sat there, seventy years old, with my heart going fast, because something had changed. That was the day I stopped being a tourist that somebody helps, and became a traveler that somebody asks. It did not take perfect grammar. It took an opinion, and one reason, and the courage to say it out loud.
